title: Warm-image GPU memory leak triggering reserved pool allocation failures
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Multiple customer escalations reported intermittent 503s and long tail latency for Dedicated tenants during scheduled warmup windows. Initial alerts pointed at reserved pool allocation failures and rapid eviction of pre-warmed workers. Investigation shows unusual GPU memory usage growth on pre-warmed container images which reduced effective headroom and caused the allocator to deny burst allocations. This ticket tracks investigation, immediate mitigations, hotfix, and broader preventive work.
impact_summary: Between 2026-03-01 07:10 UTC and 2026-03-01 11:45 UTC, affected tenants saw failed burst allocations and elevated request latencies. Approximately 8 tenants (inc. AcmeHealth and OrbitPay) experienced degraded throughput; three escalated to Success/Support. Estimated customer-visible error budget consumption: ~2.3% for Dedicated tier across the window. Severity: high for impacted tenants (service interruptions during peak warmup).

2026-03-01 07:18 UTC: support ticket from AcmeHealth reporting 503s
2026-03-01 08:00 UTC: initial mitigation: throttle burst admissions to avoid allocator thrash
2026-03-01 09:15 UTC: engineering oncall reproduced headroom drop locally using warm-image workload
2026-03-01 10:30 UTC: Hotfix v1 deployed to eu-west-1 (container GC patch)
2026-03-01 11:40 UTC: allocator headroom stabilized; customer errors reduced

reproduction_steps:
1) Deploy a pre-warmed container with our standard warm-image (inference runtime + model shard preloaded).
2) Send a steady ramp of short chat requests that exercise model loading paths for ~90 seconds, then pause 30s, repeat.
3) Observe GPU memory usage rising across repeated warm cycles; KV cache not accounting for image-heap allocations.
4) Trigger allocator decision; reserved pool admission fails when perceived free GPU memory < threshold despite nominal capacity.
technical_findings:
- The warm-image startup flow allocates pinned GPU buffers for model shard prefetching. Under test the buffer lifetime extended beyond expected GC window due to a refcount leak in the image preloader.
- Memory instrumentation used by allocator pulls from process cgroups and GPU driver reports; the preloader allocates via low-level nvml/cuda APIs bypassing our accounting layer, leading to allocator underestimation of usable headroom.
- When measurable free GPU memory dipped under the burst threshold, the reserved pool admission rejected requests resulting in burst denials and fallbacks to slower cold pools or 503s if fallback capacity exhausted.
- The issue was most prominent in pools with many pre-warmed images and in regions using older NVIDIA driver 520.x where the driver delayed memory release signals by ~2s, amplifying the leak effect.
root_cause: A reference-counting bug in the warm-image preloader caused persistent pinned GPU allocations that bypassed allocator accounting (nvml direct allocations). Combined with a driver-side delay in freeing memory signals, effective headroom was reduced and the reserved pool admission logic rejected burst allocations. The allocator behaved as designed given incorrect free-memory inputs.
mitigation:
Hotfix v1: added a conservative cgroup-level GPU memory floor for reserved pool admission to prevent rapid denial during warm cycles; deployed to eu-west-1 2026-03-01 10:30 UTC. Also added an emergency GC trigger to force deallocation of preloader buffers after 45s of idleness.
Operational mitigation: temporarily increased burst headroom threshold for impacted pools and enabled a short soft-fallback window to allow cold pool routing instead of immediate 503s.
deployment_plan:
1) Roll hotfix PRs to a single small AZ in eu-west-1; monitor allocator headroom and customer error rate for 60m.
2) If stable, roll to remaining AZs in eu-west-1 (canary → region).
3) Roll to us-west-2 and ap-south-1 with extended watch windows.
4) Coordinate with infra to schedule driver bump to 525.x in next maintenance window to remove driver-delay amplification.

follow_up_actions: 1. Implement permanent allocator accounting for direct nvml allocations (runtime-1.21).
2. Add end-to-end warm-image lifecycle tests that assert no persistent pinned allocations after idle window (Cycle 42).
3. Driver upgrade plan and validation matrix for affected regions.
4. Update runbooks: include warm-image GC and admission-floor thresholds in Reserved Pool incidents.
5. Postmortem and post-deployment evaluation to quantify residual customer error budget impact.
